title: Antigone
author: Sophocles
tagline: Sophocles’ play, with Greek-based commentary and reflections for reading across translations.
coverIntro: Below is the whole play, divided where a Greek tragedy divides itself: the prologue, the entry of the Chorus, then episodes with a choral ode after each, and the exodos. Each section is a landing on the trail. The faint arcs are where my notes reach across the play. Click a landing and start reading; lines underlined in red carry my notes, and each section ends with what I make of it.
crewIntro: The persons of the drama. Click a first appearance to go there.
about: The displayed text is F. Storr’s 1912 translation from Project Gutenberg, unaltered. You can also read the commentary alongside a different edition: use the scene, speaker, and highlighted passage to find the corresponding exchange.
The section titles are mine. The divisions are the play’s own; a Greek audience felt each one as the Chorus began to sing. There are {sections} sections here, with a reading of each.

The {notes} line notes explain the dramatic situation, Greek words where they illuminate the passage, and choices a translation may make. Select a highlighted passage to read its commentary in the side panel. Selected passages also compare possible English renderings with R. C. Jebb’s translation preserved by Perseus. The alternative glosses and first-person reflections are this companion’s interpretations, not quotations from unnamed editions. Greek line references can vary slightly with editorial line divisions.

The play was first performed in Athens around 441 BC. Its story comes last in the Theban cycle, after Oedipus the King, though Sophocles wrote it more than a decade earlier. Its ending was no secret to its first audience and the notes do not treat it as one.

movements.name: The Edict and the Deed
movements.desc: A new king forbids a burial, a sister resolves on it in the dark, and the city wakes to find the thing already done by no visible hand.

movements.name: The Collision
movements.desc: Antigone and then Haemon argue with Creon face to face, and each exchange leaves him with a narrower reason and a harsher sentence.

movements.name: The Living Tomb
movements.desc: Antigone is led away mourning the life she will not have, doubting for the first time, while the elders can offer her only old stories.

movements.name: The Reckoning
movements.desc: The prophet breaks Creon in a few minutes, Creon hurries to undo everything in the wrong order, and his house falls on him.

context.author: Sophocles (c. 496–406 BC) was a playwright and public figure in Athens. He competed in the city’s dramatic festivals and also served in political and military office. Seven of his tragedies survive complete.
context.world: Greek tragedy was a public experience, performed at festivals of Dionysus. Actors and a singing, dancing chorus brought heroic myths before an Athenian audience. Family obligations and civic authority could be debated in the same theatrical space.

worldSource.label: The Met · Theater in ancient Greece

context.importance:
Antigone sets two obligations against one another: the duty to bury a brother and the duty to obey the city. Its power comes from making the disagreement costly and personal. A ruler’s decree reaches into a family; a private act becomes a public challenge.

The play keeps returning to questions that outlive its ancient setting: when should conscience resist authority, who gets to speak for a community, and what happens when certainty makes listening impossible? Read for the arguments, but also for the people those arguments leave exposed.

context.readingGuide: Reading another translation? Follow the speaker and exchange rather than matching the English word for word. The notes use Greek line references and, at selected passages, compare translation choices with Jebb. The displayed translation is F. Storr’s.

references.name: Oedipus
references.role: Father of Antigone and Ismene; the former king of Thebes.
references.desc: The former king of Thebes and father of Antigone, Ismene, Eteocles and Polyneices. In the family's earlier story he blinded himself and went into exile. His suffering and the troubled inheritance of his household form part of the background the sisters share.

references.name: Jocasta
references.desc: The former queen of Thebes, mother of Antigone and her siblings, and sister of Creon. Her marriage to Oedipus belongs to the family's painful earlier history. Remembering that she is Creon's sister explains why the new king is the children's uncle.

references.name: Polyneices
references.role: Brother of Antigone and Ismene. Creon has forbidden his burial after he attacked Thebes.
references.desc: One of Antigone's brothers, who brought an army against Thebes in the struggle for its throne. He and his brother Eteocles have killed each other before the play begins. Creon treats him as an enemy of the city and forbids his burial; Antigone continues to see him as a brother to whom she owes a sacred duty.

references.name: Eteocles
references.role: Brother of Antigone and Ismene; he died fighting Polyneices for Thebes.
references.desc: Antigone's brother, who defended Thebes against the army led by Polyneices. The brothers killed each other before the opening scene. Creon grants him an honored burial as the city's defender, making the contrast with Polyneices central to the play's dispute about kinship and public loyalty.
